The question is no longer if this virus can harm Australian wildlife, but whether we should use every available tool to protect species most at risk. Vaccination cannot stop H5N1 spreading through wildlife. But it could prevent an outbreak from killing all of the at-risk species in an area – a tragic local extinction. Australia should begin targeted vaccination of threatened birds. It should also urgently develop a strategy for seals and sea lions, rather than waiting until thousands are dead. A policy exists, but action remains too cautious Australia has a national policy that allows emergency vaccination of rare, protected and valuable birds, including animals in zoos, sanctuaries, breeding programs and some managed wild populations. The government has also purchased an inactivated H5 vaccine – containing no live virus – and is running pilot studies in captive non-poultry birds. This is important groundwork, but not yet a public program comparable with New Zealand’s ambitious and proactive approach to vaccinate five of the country’s rarest birds before the arrival of H5N1. Australian zoos and sanctuaries have received funding to strengthen biosecurity and captive “insurance populations”. Pilot vaccinations are underway, but the government has not announced which threatened species will receive wider vaccination, where, or when. More importantly, the policy excludes non-avian (bird) species, meaning marine mammals are not considered despite their known vulnerability to H5N1. No plans have been announced to the public for Australian vaccination trials for seals or sea lions. What overseas programs show New Zealand prepared before H5N1 arrived. After species-specific trials, it began vaccinating about 300 core breeding birds of rare species, including kākāpō, takahē and black stilts. These are captive or closely managed populations whose individuals can be found, vaccinated twice and monitored. The United States acted after H5N1 killed 21 critically endangered California condors. By October 2024, 207 captive and free-flying condors had been vaccinated. The vaccine was judged safe, although two birds had treatable adverse reactions. France has conducted a vaccine trial in wild king penguin chicks on the French sub-Antarctic island of Crozet. The vaccine produced strong, virus-neutralising antibodies without detected adverse effects. These programs do not prove vaccination will prevent every infection. But it could lessen severe disease and reduce the number of animals that die in threatened populations. The marine mammals most at risk are the sea lion, fur seal and elephant seal, while the Tasmanian devil and eastern quoll (pictured) are the highest-risk species on land. Rexness/flickr, CC BY Which species should Australia vaccinate? Broadscale vaccination of free-ranging wildlife is unrealistic. Most H5 vaccines require two doses, and most wildlife is difficult to capture once, let alone being recaptured for a booster and blood test. The best candidates are small populations of at-risk species that are either easily accessible or already under management. For example, threatened birds in zoos or breeding centres, or small, known colonies with tracking or regular handling. On Tuesday, the Australian government released a list of at-risk species, that showed almost one-in-five Australian bird and mammal species is at high, very high or extreme risk from the virus. Five bird species are at extreme risk – the Christmas Island frigate bird, Houtman albatross, Herald petrel, imperial shag on Heard Island and imperial shag on Macquarie Island. The marine mammals most at risk are the sea lion, fur seal and elephant seal, while the Tasmanian devil and eastern quoll are the highest risk species on land. Decisions must balance extinction risk, exposure to the virus, cost, vaccine performance, whether enough animals can be reached, and whether capture would cause unacceptable stress. Vaccination must sit alongside existing biosecurity, surveillance and conservation measures – not replace them. Australia needs a seal plan H5N1 has decimated seal and sea lion populations across South America and the Southern Ocean. More than 17,000 southern elephant seal pups were killed in Argentina in 2023. An estimated 13,359 pups died at the Australian sub-Antarctic Heard Island in 2025, believed to be from the virus. Southern elephant seals were listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List in April, in part because of the catastrophic mortality caused by bird flu. It will take decades for these populations to recover. Australia’s most vulnerable seals include the endangered Australian sea lion, Australian and long-nosed fur seals, and southern elephant seals. H5N1-positive terns have already been found at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island, home to a major Australian sea lion breeding colony. Southern elephant seals have a large breeding colony on Australia’s sub-Antarctic Macquarie Island, which remains free of H5N1 at this time. There is currently no bird flu vaccine designed specifically for marine mammals. A United States trial aimed at protecting endangered Hawaiian monk seals found a vaccine developed for cattle was safe in northern elephant seals and produced measurable antibodies. This was the closest comparable species for which a safe, conditionally licensed vaccine was available. Developing and approving a separate vaccine for every wildlife species is costly and time-consuming, so conservation programs commonly adapt vaccines already approved for domestic animals. Now is the time to act Australia should identify priority seal colonies now, trial candidate vaccines in a suitable surrogate species and plan how vaccination could be deployed. We should not wait to learn how susceptible these animals are by watching more mass deaths unfold. Vaccination is not a silver bullet. But when a disease can erase years of conservation work in weeks, we should not wait for perfect certainty. It’s time to act before catastrophe. A harpy eagle needs large trees for nesting and enough surrounding forest for its young to learn to fly. The Amazon also depends on the eagle. By controlling populations of monkeys, sloths, and other animals, the predator helps limit damage to the forest canopy. Its decline can therefore indicate broader changes in the ecosystem. Governments often assess biodiversity by counting species. These figures are useful, although they don’t show whether an ecosystem is still functioning. A recent paper in Frontiers in Science argues that conservation policy should also track ecological processes, including predation, migration, pollination, and the movement of water and nutrients, reports Mongabay’s John Cannon. The authors propose using the Three Global Conditions Framework, developed in 2019, to decide what different landscapes require. It divides the planet according to the degree of human influence. Large, relatively intact areas need protection from new development. Landscapes where farming and settlements coexist with nature require management that maintains ecological functions. Heavily altered areas need restoration. The approach could help countries meet the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which calls for the loss of nature to be halted and reversed by 2030. Progress varies widely among countries. The agreement is not legally binding, and national governments determine how its targets are applied. The paper uses the term “nature positive” to describe an outcome in which ecosystems are healthier at the end of the decade than they were at its start. Measuring this will be difficult. An increase in tree cover, for example, may reveal little about whether a restored forest supports its former species or ecological relationships. Implementation also raises political and economic questions. Conservation measures can restrict access to land, change farming practices, or impose costs on communities that contributed little to biodiversity loss. Decisions about what to protect and restore will depend partly on whose knowledge is recognized and who bears the expense. The framework helps distinguish among landscapes and identify suitable forms of intervention. Governments will still need to turn broad targets into policies that reflect local conditions, maintain ecological functions, and allocate costs in ways that affected communities consider fair. On a Philippine beach, villagers are stepping up to save sea turtle nests Mongabay.com 6 Aug 2026 Beaches in San Vicente municipality in the Philippines’ Palawan province are crucial nesting grounds for olive ridley sea turtles. But the turtles and their babies face perilous journeys on those beaches — from dogs, tourism, and increasingly severe storms and high tides. To counter these threats, the NGO Large Marine Vertebrates Research Institute Philippines (LAMAVE) has partnered with residents to patrol the beaches and rescue turtle eggs, reports contributor Rachel Duckett for Mongabay. In Santo Niño village, volunteers and patrollers conduct intensive night patrols covering more than 8 kilometers (5 mile) of the beach in five shifts. When the patrollers find a nesting turtle, they protect her from dogs. When she’s done nesting, they measure her and take photographs of her before she reenters the water. These help them identify her in the future. Then they relocate the eggs to protected hatcheries, a move researchers say is vital because nests left on the beach are almost always lost to stray dogs or flooding. Sometimes, they encounter dead nesting mothers or turtles mortally wounded by dogs. They remove eggs from those nests as well. “In the end, even though she’s dead, at least her babies survive,” said researcher Klara Simon at LAMAVE. In the hatcheries, the eggs are placed in nests in the sand, which the researchers check on every few hours. Baby olive ridleys (Lepidochelys olivacea) start emerging two months after the eggs are laid. According to LAMAVE data from last season and preliminary data from this season, their hatcheries achieve a hatching success rate of approximately 75%. For comparison, on beaches untouched by predators, hatching success rates of 80% or higher are common for olive ridley nests. Local patrollers like Jerald Mahusay, who once viewed turtle eggs as toys during his childhood, now serve as research assistants and patrol leaders. LAMAVE also engages directly with residents to manage free-roaming dogs, such as building enclosures for pets that might otherwise attack turtles and eat the eggs. Despite the current reliance on hatcheries, project leader Kalei Suza said relocation is a temporary measure necessitated by human-induced pressures. “We still want the turtles to nest in their regular, natural place where they want to nest, because mama knows best,” Suza said, noting that the ultimate goal is for the community to take full ownership of turtle protection. San Vicente has seen a rise in tourism over the last few years. Luxury developer Century Properties purchased 56 hectares (138 acres) of land in the municipality with plans to build a beachfront resort. Another major developer, Megaworld Corporation, has begun construction of a resort expected to cover 462 hectares (1,142 acres). Read the full story by Rachel Duckett here. In Manila’s shadow, a forest refuge still shelters rare plants Naina Rao 6 Aug 2026 A mountainous reserve near Manila, the Philippine capital, is a critical ecological refuge, harboring high levels of plant diversity despite its proximity to the highly urbanized city, according to a recent study. The findings come from surveys done 10 years earlier, however, and mounting pressures on the area’s forests since then may have had an impact, the authors say. As the last remaining natural lowland forest in Cavite province, on the southern shores of Manila Bay, Mounts Palay-palay-Mataas-na-Gulod Protected Landscape serves as a vital stronghold for Philippine biodiversity, researchers say. In July 2016, they surveyed plants within the landscape, known as MPPMGPL. At the time, they documented 294 species of plants across the landscape’s varied habitats, from grasslands and secondary forests to old-growth stands. They found that 42 species, or 16%, are found only in the Philippines, while 31 species are classified as threatened on national or international red lists. “The most remarkable finding is that this landscape ... harbors an incredibly high concentration of biodiversity despite being so close to highly urbanized zones,” study lead author Enrico Replan, an assistant professor at the Institute of Environmental Science and Meteorology (IESM) at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told Mongabay by email. The study also identified 43 species that likely represent new records for Cavite province, “filling major geographic knowledge gaps,” Replan said. Among the most significant findings was the dominance of guijo (Shorea guiso), a critically endangered tree species, in the forest’s interior core. This highlights the role of MPPMGPL as a key conservation refuge, the authors write. While the study was only published recently, Replan told Mongabay the 2016 findings offer a baseline for this landscape; there haven’t been similar surveys since. In the past 10 years, however, urbanization and land conversion have led to a decrease in forested areas and breached strict protection zones in the landscape. A study that used satellite imagery to examine changes in forest area from 2015 to 2021, found a 13.8% decrease in MPPMGPL due to urbanization. The 2016 survey “showed promising resurgence of Shorea guiso” in the interior core parts of MPPMGPL, Replan said. But because dipterocarp species such as guijo are highly sensitive to local climatic changes and canopy gaps, he added that any encroachment that disturbed the forest over the last decade could easily have stalled this progress. “This 10-year gap highlights exactly why we are calling for continuous, long-term monitoring rather than relying solely on spatial snapshots,” Replan said. He added that stricter local policy interventions and aggressive conservation programs are urgently needed to safeguard the endemic and threatened plants in the landscape “before they are permanently fragmented or lost.” The research team writes that establishing permanent monitoring plots would better track the functional dynamics of this ecosystem amidst climate change. Image courtesy of Enrico Replan. What happens after a whale strands on a Mumbai beach? Stephin Thomas 6 Aug 2026 On the morning of June 27, a 7.6-meter (25-foot) blue whale calf washed ashore on a busy beach in Mumbai, India’s financial capital and the capital of Maharashtra state. Whale strandings are rare along the Maharashtra coast, so Mongabay spoke with experts to find out what happened next. “Each stranding incident is a totally unexpected event,” N. Vasudevan, former head of Maharashtra government’s Mangrove Cell, an administrative unit that manages coastal ecosystems, told Mongabay. “You can prepare for years, but then it may not happen for years. And one fine morning, it is there on the beach.” According to the Mangrove Foundation, a registered society established by the Maharashtra government, only six of the 109 recorded stranding incidents in 2020-21 involved whales. Under national guidelines, the first step in any stranding involving a protected species, such as the blue whale (Balaenoptera musculus), is alerting the local stranding network, whose coordinator notifies the forest department, according to Shaunak Modi, director of the Coastal Conservation Foundation, which is also part of the Mumbai Stranding Response Network. Modi said that on June 27, a lifeguard notified him about the whale calf around 9 a.m. By the time he reached the site in the Bandra coastline 30 minutes later, the young cetacean had suffered severe injuries from crashing against exposed rocks. Ultimately, police and fire department authorities at the site confirmed it had died. Fishers and local people told Modi they had first spotted the stranded whale around 6 a.m. First responders, primarily local fishers and lifeguards, receive specialized training to inform the network immediately of these emergencies, he said. But what happens to the dead whale? Modi said legal and practical realities clash under national law. The blue whale is a Schedule 1 species, meaning authorities give it the highest-level protection in India. “As per the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, if any Schedule 1 species dies, it needs to be cremated,” Modi said. But the law was made with terrestrial animals in mind, he added. “If you try to burn a whale, I can assure you it will keep burning for days, if not weeks, because it has that much oil in it. So then instead of cremating a marine mammal, they’re buried.” The calf was buried in a Mumbai beach. Beforehand, veterinarians collected tissue samples and conducted a necropsy under forest department supervision. “The necropsy report is still not ready, but what we know is that it was a calf,” Modi said. “Blue whale calves stay with their mother for up to seven or eight years and are entirely dependent on her for food during the first few years. We assume it may have been separated from its mother, which caused its condition.” Vasudevan said there are systematic hurdles in knowing the cause of death. “The experts who conduct necropsy are nonexistent in our country.” Banner image: Stranded whale calf in Mumbai. Image courtesy of Shaunak Modi. Social media images lead to first recording of parasitoid wasp species in Japan David Brown 6 Aug 2026 Photos of a striking, iridescent wasp posted on social media by wasp enthusiasts in Japan have led to an unexpected discovery: The images are the first record of the species in Japan. The footage also helped scientists describe a male of the species for the first time. The images and a video of the wasps were posted by two citizen scientists on Twitter (now X) in 2018 and 2021. The video showed a female wasp depositing her eggs onto a hard egg case of a praying mantis. Taisuke Kawano, a wasp expert at the Kyushu University Museum, Japan, noticed the footage and contacted the wasp enthusiasts who then sent him a few specimens of the wasp. The citizen scientists are also co-authors of a study, published in June, that details the scientists’ findings. Kawano and his colleagues identified the wasp as Eupelmus curvator. It’s a parasitoid wasp that lays its eggs in the egg cases of mantises. The larvae of the wasps feed on the mantis eggs as they develop. The researchers said the photos posted on social media are the first known record of Eupelmus curvator in Japan. The species was previously known only from China. The researchers were also able to scientifically describe the E. curvator male for the first time. Only the female of the species was previously described. According to LAMAVE data from last season and preliminary data from this season, their hatcheries achieve a hatching success rate of approximately 75%. For comparison, on beaches untouched by predators, hatching success rates of 80% or higher are common for olive ridley nests. Local patrollers like Jerald Mahusay, who once viewed turtle eggs as toys during his childhood, now serve as research assistants and patrol leaders. LAMAVE also engages directly with residents to manage free-roaming dogs, such as building enclosures for pets that might otherwise attack turtles and eat the eggs. Despite the current reliance on hatcheries, project leader Kalei Suza said relocation is a temporary measure necessitated by human-induced pressures. “We still want the turtles to nest in their regular, natural place where they want to nest, because mama knows best,” Suza said, noting that the ultimate goal is for the community to take full ownership of turtle protection. San Vicente has seen a rise in tourism over the last few years. Luxury developer Century Properties purchased 56 hectares (138 acres) of land in the municipality with plans to build a beachfront resort. Another major developer, Megaworld Corporation, has begun construction of a resort expected to cover 462 hectares (1,142 acres). Read the full story by Rachel Duckett here. In Manila’s shadow, a forest refuge still shelters rare plants Naina Rao 6 Aug 2026 A mountainous reserve near Manila, the Philippine capital, is a critical ecological refuge, harboring high levels of plant diversity despite its proximity to the highly urbanized city, according to a recent study. The findings come from surveys done 10 years earlier, however, and mounting pressures on the area’s forests since then may have had an impact, the authors say. As the last remaining natural lowland forest in Cavite province, on the southern shores of Manila Bay, Mounts Palay-palay-Mataas-na-Gulod Protected Landscape serves as a vital stronghold for Philippine biodiversity, researchers say. In July 2016, they surveyed plants within the landscape, known as MPPMGPL. At the time, they documented 294 species of plants across the landscape’s varied habitats, from grasslands and secondary forests to old-growth stands. They found that 42 species, or 16%, are found only in the Philippines, while 31 species are classified as threatened on national or international red lists. “The most remarkable finding is that this landscape ... harbors an incredibly high concentration of biodiversity despite being so close to highly urbanized zones,” study lead author Enrico Replan, an assistant professor at the Institute of Environmental Science and Meteorology (IESM) at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told Mongabay by email. The study also identified 43 species that likely represent new records for Cavite province, “filling major geographic knowledge gaps,” Replan said. Among the most significant findings was the dominance of guijo (Shorea guiso), a critically endangered tree species, in the forest’s interior core. This highlights the role of MPPMGPL as a key conservation refuge, the authors write. While the study was only published recently, Replan told Mongabay the 2016 findings offer a baseline for this landscape; there haven’t been similar surveys since. In the past 10 years, however, urbanization and land conversion have led to a decrease in forested areas and breached strict protection zones in the landscape. A study that used satellite imagery to examine changes in forest area from 2015 to 2021, found a 13.8% decrease in MPPMGPL due to urbanization. The 2016 survey “showed promising resurgence of Shorea guiso” in the interior core parts of MPPMGPL, Replan said. But because dipterocarp species such as guijo are highly sensitive to local climatic changes and canopy gaps, he added that any encroachment that disturbed the forest over the last decade could easily have stalled this progress. “This 10-year gap highlights exactly why we are calling for continuous, long-term monitoring rather than relying solely on spatial snapshots,” Replan said. He added that stricter local policy interventions and aggressive conservation programs are urgently needed to safeguard the endemic and threatened plants in the landscape “before they are permanently fragmented or lost.” The research team writes that establishing permanent monitoring plots would better track the functional dynamics of this ecosystem amidst climate change. Image courtesy of Enrico Replan. What happens after a whale strands on a Mumbai beach? Stephin Thomas 6 Aug 2026 On the morning of June 27, a 7.6-meter (25-foot) blue whale calf washed ashore on a busy beach in Mumbai, India’s financial capital and the capital of Maharashtra state. Whale strandings are rare along the Maharashtra coast, so Mongabay spoke with experts to find out what happened next. “Each stranding incident is a totally unexpected event,” N. Vasudevan, former head of Maharashtra government’s Mangrove Cell, an administrative unit that manages coastal ecosystems, told Mongabay. “You can prepare for years, but then it may not happen for years. And one fine morning, it is there on the beach.” According to the Mangrove Foundation, a registered society established by the Maharashtra government, only six of the 109 recorded stranding incidents in 2020-21 involved whales. Under national guidelines, the first step in any stranding involving a protected species, such as the blue whale (Balaenoptera musculus), is alerting the local stranding network, whose coordinator notifies the forest department, according to Shaunak Modi, director of the Coastal Conservation Foundation, which is also part of the Mumbai Stranding Response Network. Modi said that on June 27, a lifeguard notified him about the whale calf around 9 a.m. By the time he reached the site in the Bandra coastline 30 minutes later, the young cetacean had suffered severe injuries from crashing against exposed rocks. Ultimately, police and fire department authorities at the site confirmed it had died. Fishers and local people told Modi they had first spotted the stranded whale around 6 a.m. First responders, primarily local fishers and lifeguards, receive specialized training to inform the network immediately of these emergencies, he said. But what happens to the dead whale? Modi said legal and practical realities clash under national law. The blue whale is a Schedule 1 species, meaning authorities give it the highest-level protection in India. “As per the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, if any Schedule 1 species dies, it needs to be cremated,” Modi said. But the law was made with terrestrial animals in mind, he added. “If you try to burn a whale, I can assure you it will keep burning for days, if not weeks, because it has that much oil in it. So then instead of cremating a marine mammal, they’re buried.” The calf was buried in a Mumbai beach. Beforehand, veterinarians collected tissue samples and conducted a necropsy under forest department supervision. “The necropsy report is still not ready, but what we know is that it was a calf,” Modi said. “Blue whale calves stay with their mother for up to seven or eight years and are entirely dependent on her for food during the first few years. We assume it may have been separated from its mother, which caused its condition.” Vasudevan said there are systematic hurdles in knowing the cause of death. “The experts who conduct necropsy are nonexistent in our country.” Banner image: Stranded whale calf in Mumbai. Social media images lead to first recording of parasitoid wasp species in Japan David Brown 6 Aug 2026 Photos of a striking, iridescent wasp posted on social media by wasp enthusiasts in Japan have led to an unexpected discovery: The images are the first record of the species in Japan. The footage also helped scientists describe a male of the species for the first time. The images and a video of the wasps were posted by two citizen scientists on Twitter (now X) in 2018 and 2021. The video showed a female wasp depositing her eggs onto a hard egg case of a praying mantis. Taisuke Kawano, a wasp expert at the Kyushu University Museum, Japan, noticed the footage and contacted the wasp enthusiasts who then sent him a few specimens of the wasp. The citizen scientists are also co-authors of a study, published in June, that details the scientists’ findings. Kawano and his colleagues identified the wasp as Eupelmus curvator. It’s a parasitoid wasp that lays its eggs in the egg cases of mantises. The larvae of the wasps feed on the mantis eggs as they develop. The researchers said the photos posted on social media are the first known record of Eupelmus curvator in Japan. The species was previously known only from China. The researchers were also able to scientifically describe the E. curvator male for the first time. Only the female of the species was previously described. For the second year in a row, visitors to the Butler Farm Show can expect to see the finest live duck, chicken and turkey exhibits — but only from a safe distance. Jordan Kennedy, who is in charge of poultry events at the Butler Farm Show, said event organizers are following Pennsylvania guidelines on managing highly pathologic avian influenza, or HPAI. The guidelines were slightly loosened last year, just enough to allow the farm show to include poultry showmanship for the first time since 2019. “The farm show is doing everything it can to give opportunities to families and kids; and we’re doing everything we can within the Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture's requirements to allow these kids to show and exhibit the animals they work so hard on,” Kennedy said. Ken Metrick, Butler Farm Show board secretary, was in charge of the Butler County 4-H Poultry Club in 2019. He has chickens at his Harvest View Farm in Butler Township. Butler Eagle File Photo As a result of restrictions imposed by the Department of Agriculture, the public will not be allowed into the poultry tent, but will be allowed to look at the birds from a distance. “The Department of Agriculture requires us to have a buffer or quarantine zone between the birds and the public, so there will be no public allowed to go into the poultry tent,” Kennedy said. “We're going to try and have the tent as open as possible so that folks can see into the tent.” Visitors can rest assured all birds exhibited at the Farm Show are prescreened for avian flu and other illnesses, according to Kennedy. “Every bird that's on the grounds that's being exhibited has to be tested for diseases and sicknesses, including avian influenza, just to ensure that all the birds and people are as safe as possible,” Kennedy said. Due to tighter restrictions against avian influenza, poultry exhibits were entirely absent from the farm show from 2021 to 2024. Combined with the 2020 show, which was canceled entirely due to the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, that marked five straight seasons in which Butler County’s young poultry farmers were unable to display their work at the farm show. During those years, the farm show filled the poultry tent with educational displays and posters. While they may have a tough time getting a good look at what’s going on, visitors can look forward to the traditional poultry showcases this year, as well as a new one: market turkey. The poultry show is scheduled at 9 a.m. Tuesday, Aug. 11, with poultry showmanship scheduled for 9 a.m. the following day. “We have our usual poultry show where the show birds will be judged,” Kennedy said. “All your different breeds and ages of poultry, whether it be large chicken, bantam chicken, large duck, bantam duck, geese, turkeys.” Lily Williams, a Butler Area High School junior, shows off the Butler County 4-H poultry club’s turkey on Saturday, Aug. 9, 2025, at the Butler Farm Show. The bird was 35 pounds and 17 weeks old. Matthew Glover/Butler Eagle In addition, turkeys and meat pens (a type of chicken) are among the types of livestock which will be auctioned off at the Farm Show’s annual Junior Livestock Sale on Thursday, Aug. 13. Unlike the poultry tent, the livestock sale will be open to the public. “Those turkeys will be shown by the kids, judged by an official judge and then sold Thursday night at the livestock auction,” Kennedy said. This year’s Farm Show also marks the return of two popular poultry-related events — the rooster crowing contest, scheduled for 4 p.m. Wednesday, Aug. 12, and the poultry costume contest, scheduled for 4 p.m. Friday, Aug. 14. While the costume contest has been around for “quite a few years” according to Kennedy, the rooster crowing contest is entering its second year after a successful debut in 2025. “The 4-H Poultry Club has grown and is still growing,” Kennedy said. “The rooster crowing contest and the costume contest are both set up to give these kids another opportunity to work with their animals and enjoy themselves. We hope that as many kids as possible participate, but it's a busy week for a lot of those kids.” Keira Cardin plays sounds from her phone to get her rooster to crow during the rooster crowing contest at the 77th annual Butler Farm Show on Wednesday, Aug. 6, 2025.
